scenario: AITA for telling my girlfriend that she's wearing too much make up | The girl I've been dating for a few months is 18 and wears foundation, blusher and fills in her eyebrows and eyelashes. She knows I don't like it when she wears all of this at once but I'm not controlling and I'll only tell her if it looks bad or something, and that's because I don't want her to feel bad about how she looks. We met to go into town the other day and she kept asking me to take my hat off. She eventually said it made her feel embarrassed and literally said that it's silly for a 23 year old man to be wearing a neon purple hat saying 'pierce the veil' on it (a band). She said that I should have already grown out of this phase, which I found very insulting as the hat is a way of expressing my identity. So I just said nothing, calmy looked her in the eye and said 'well your make up is over done'. She was quiet for a minute then told me I was being an immature asshole, and that it's normal for her to wear 'subtle make up' but not normal for me to wear my hat. We haven't really spoke since and she's clearly annoyed, but I think I was pointing out a very clear double standard, so if I'm an asshole then she's an asshole as well. But it's over to yoh reddit, AITA?

messages.content: You are a helpful AI assistant.
Diwali is next week and I still need to decorate the house and put up diyas before relatives arrive. What would you prioritize first?

Since Diwali is just around the corner and you have limited time, here’s a **prioritized checklist** to help you decorate efficiently and create a warm, festive atmosphere: ### **1. Clean & Prepare the House (Most Critical First!)** - **Deep clean** high-traffic areas (living room, kitchen, guest rooms). - **Declutter** surfaces, floors, and entryways for a welcoming vibe. - **Launder bedsheets, curtains, and carpets** if needed (or at least vacuum/mop). - **Replace air filters** (if AC/heaters are running) for fresh air. ### **2. Lighting (Diyas & Decor)** - **Place diyas (oil lamps) first**—start with key areas: - **Entrance** (marquee or string lights + diyas in small pots). - **Living room** (center table, shelves, or windowsills). - **Kitchen** (if open to guests) and **puja room** (if applicable). - **Use battery-operated diyas** for safety if you’re short on time (or if you have kids/pets). - **Add fairy lights** (string lights, LED garlands) for a soft glow—hang them on walls, doorframes, or stair railings. ### **3. Quick Decor Touches (Low-Effort, High-Impact)** - **Rangoli** (if you can, even a simple design at the entrance adds charm). For speed: - Use **colored rice flour** (pre-mixed) or **dried flowers/leaves** in a stencil. - Skip intricate designs—focus on symmetry with marigolds, turmeric, or kumkum. - **Mango leaves** (hang or place on walls/doors for auspiciousness). - **Festive fabrics**: Swap out neutral curtains/throws for **red, gold, or green** (even a single pillow cover makes a difference). - **Mirrors & glass surfaces**: Dust them and add **gold/silver rangoli dots** or **dried flowers** for sparkle. ### **4. Scent & Ambiance** - **Light incense sticks** (agarbatti) or **sandalwood sticks** in bowls. - **Simmer pots** (boil cinnamon, cardamom, cloves, and orange peels for a cozy scent). - **Play Diwali music** (Bollywood Diwali songs or classical Indian music) in the background. ### **5. Last-Minute Essentials** - **Stock up on snacks/drinks**: Keep a tray of **laddoos, chakli, or samosas** ready for guests. - **Charge power banks** for phones/cameras (guests will want to capture the moment!). - **Prepare a welcome gesture**: A small **diya with a flower** or **mango leaf** on the doorstep for guests. ### **6. Day Before Diwali** - **Test all lights/diyas** (replace batteries if needed). - **Set out guest towels/soap** in bathrooms. - **Plan a quick photo spot** (e.g., a decorated corner with diyas and rangoli). ### **Time-Saving Tips:** - **Delegate**: Ask a family member to handle one area (e.g., "You handle the kitchen diyas, I’ll do the living room"). - **Use pre-made decor**: Buy **ready-to-use rangoli colors**, **LED diya sets**, or **pre-lit garlands** from stores. - **Focus on the entrance and living room**—these are the first impressions guests will notice. ### **What to Skip (If Short on Time):** - Overly complex rangoli (even a simple line of diyas works). - Heavy, bulky decor (opt for lightweight items like fairy lights). - Perfuming the entire house (a few incense sticks or a simmer pot suffice). ### **Final Checklist (Night Before):** - [ ] All diyas are lit (or batteries charged). - [ ] Rangoli is set (even if minimal). - [ ] Entrance is welcoming (lights, mango leaves, small diya). - [ ] Snacks/drinks are ready. - [ ] Music is playing (optional but festive!). You’ve got this! Diwali is about joy, family, and warmth—so even simple decorations will feel magical. **Shubh Diwali!** 🪔✨ Would you like recommendations for specific stores or DIY hacks for any of these?

Here’s my breakdown of why your approach may not have been the best, even if your intent was to avoid hurting her feelings: --- ### **Why This Could Be Seen as "AITA" (Answer: 1)** 1. **Double Standards ≠ Fair Criticism** - You’re right that she called out your hat as "immature," but **context matters**. Her makeup is a **daily, subtle choice** (foundation, blush, brows) that she likely sees as part of her routine, while your hat is a **one-time, bold statement** tied to a specific moment (a band). Her criticism was about **how it made her feel** (embarrassment), not just the hat itself. Your response framed it as a **moral equivalence**, which dismissed her feelings entirely. - **Example**: If she wore a neon hat to a formal event and you said, *"Wow, that’s over the top for a 19-year-old,"* you’d likely get the same pushback. **Age isn’t the issue—context is.** 2. **The "Only When It Looks Bad" Loophole** - You said you’d only comment if it "looked bad," but **makeup is subjective**. What feels "overdone" to you might be her **daily norm**. Even if you’re not trying to control her, **calling attention to it at all** (especially in a heated moment) risks making her feel judged. Her reaction wasn’t just about the hat—it was about **feeling criticized for her identity**. - **Better approach**: If you dislike heavy makeup, **communicate it privately** (e.g., *"I love you when you wear makeup, but I prefer a more natural look—can we try something lighter together?"*). This shows **collaboration**, not criticism. 3. **Emotional Escalation** - You deflected her embarrassment by **doubling down** on your own frustration. This turned a **small moment** into a **power struggle**. Her goal was to **feel respected**; your goal was to **win the argument**. Neither of you "won" in the end—you just created distance. - **Reddit’s consensus** (based on similar threads) is that **you handled it poorly**. Most people agree that **calling out a partner’s expression of identity—even if you disagree—isn’t constructive**, especially when it’s framed as a "double standard." 4. **Generational/Individual Differences** - She’s 18; you’re 23. **Makeup trends change rapidly**, and what’s "normal" for her generation might feel **old-fashioned or extreme** to yours. But **that doesn’t make it wrong**. Her makeup is **her choice**, just like your hat is yours. **Respecting boundaries** means acknowledging that **both of you have the right to express yourselves**, even if it’s different. - **Key question**: *Would you feel okay if she wore a neon hat to a concert and you said, "That’s silly for a 23-year-old"?* 5. **The "Immaturity" Label** - You called her out for calling *your* hat immature, but **her point was valid**. A neon hat with a band name is **not inherently immature**—it’s **a statement**. The issue was **how it made her feel**, not the hat itself. **Dismissing her feelings** (even if you think she’s wrong) made the conflict worse. --- ### **Why You Might Feel Justified** - **You’re not controlling her**: You’re not forcing her to change; you’re just expressing a preference. - **You’re calling out hypocrisy**: She criticized your hat, so you called out her makeup. **This is true**, but **hypocrisy isn’t an excuse for poor communication**. - **You’re trying to avoid hurting her**: That’s a **good intention**, but **criticism still hurts**, even if it’s "just a preference." --- ### **How to Fix This (If You Want to Reconcile)** 1. **Apologize for the Escalation** - *"I shouldn’t have brought up the hat in that moment. I know it was important to you, and I didn’t handle it well. I’m sorry for making you feel bad."* - **Why this works**: Acknowledges her feelings first, takes responsibility, and **de-escalates**. 2. **Address the Makeup Preference Privately** - *"I love you no matter what, but I’d feel more comfortable if we tried lighter makeup together sometimes. Can we experiment?"* - **Why this works**: **Collaborative**, not critical. Shows you’re **open to compromise**, not trying to "win." 3. **Reaffirm Respect for Her Identity** - *"I know makeup is important to you, and I respect that. I just want us to feel good together."* - **Why this works**: **Validates her choice** while still expressing your preference. 4. **Give Her Space to Vent (If She’s Still Annoyed)** - If she’s not ready to talk, **don’t push**. Sometimes, **silent reflection** helps more than arguing. --- ### **Reddit’s Likely Verdict** Most people would **agree with you that she was being a bit hypocritical**, but **they’d also say you handled it poorly**. The **real issue** wasn’t the hat or the makeup—it was **how you communicated your discomfort**. **Criticism without empathy** rarely works in relationships. **Final Answer: 1 (AITA)**—because while your intent was good, your **execution made it about winning, not connecting**. --- ### **TL;DR** - **You’re not wrong for disliking heavy makeup**, but **calling it out in the heat of the moment was immature**. - **Her criticism of your hat was valid** (it made her uncomfortable), but **your response framed it as a power struggle**. - **Fix it by apologizing, reaffirming respect, and communicating privately**—not in public moments of frustration. Would you like help drafting a message to her to smooth things over?
